title: Mysterious new drug drives its users crazy
article: Growing evidence of a mysterious new street drug that turns even experienced users psychotic has police and health officials joining together to issue a warning.

Dr. Linda Poffenroth, deputy medical officer for the Capital Health Region, said Thursday that street outreach nurses and needle exchange workers are trying to spread the word about the drug, which has yet to be identified.

Poffenroth said the delusional state and violent behavior exhibited in at least three cases in Victoria indicate there is something new on the street. The symptoms resemble, but go far beyond, severe cocaine overdoses or even angel dust -- PCP.
"Whatever it is, it is one of the stimulants." she said. "There is also a chance the drugs are adulterated with something else."
Victoria police dealt Thursday with what looks like the third case of a person turned insane by this new, powerful drug.
Const. Jack McClintock said police were called out in the morning by a B.C. Transit driver to deal with a crazed
man who was clinging to the bicycle rack on the front of the bus. The man was partially clothed, screaming, and had to be restrained and taken to hospital.

Still in hospital is a woman who was arrested Tuesday morning on Balmoral Road. She was screaming, and punching parked cars. When police tried to hold her she fled and ended up on all fours trying to crawl under blackberry bushes.
The woman was so crazed that when she was finally subdued, strapped to a gurney and loaded into an ambulance, she attempted to chew through her oxygen mask.
McClintock said by Thursday afternoon neither the man nor the woman had recovered enough to talk with police, so it was not known what they thought they were taking.
A small amount of powdered substance had been seized from the man and is being tested.
"Right now we have no idea what the drug is," said McClintock.

"But there is something out there that can cause a very violent reaction." Results became available Thursday from the autopsy on Mladen Cujko, 33, a known drug user from Burnaby who died Sunday while struggling hysterically with a Western Communities RCMP officer on the Trans-Canada Highway.

The autopsy revealed Cujko did not die from any injuries received from police. Instead, he suffered some mysterious cardiac arrest. Toxicology tests are being done but results aren't expected until next week at the earliest.

RCMP Staff Sgt. Bruce Brown said also during the autopsy the pathologist located a hypodermic needle, a plastic baggy containing a white powder and some cash hidden in Cujko's clothes. The white powder and the syringe will be tested.

Brown said police will be asking lab tests to go far beyond the normal checks for standard narcotics such as cocaine, heroin or barbiturates. They want to know just what is in this stuff that is driving people insane. Lab results won't be available until next week or later.
Cujko's death is the best indicator that some strange drug is at work because a man who was with him said Cujko had taken something.
Cujko initially approached attendants at the Co-op Gas Station on Goldstream Avenue, wild-eyed and agitated and asked them to call 911.
"Bad coke," was only explanation his companion offered when one of the attendants asked him what was wrong.
Moments later Cujko was running around in traffic as though somebody was chasing him, screaming "Help me. Help me. I didn't do it. I didn't do it."
Brown said Cujko had previous convictions for drug offences and was well known to police. And that goes to show the potent danger of this new narcotic, he said.
Brown said he can't ever recall any drug that has had such a violent reaction on people.
"These are experienced drug users who are getting into trouble," he said.
"This is a prime example of why you shouldn't take drugs."
